name: Standing Single-Leg Balance Reach
description: The single-leg balance reach challenges proprioception and neuromuscular control by requiring the exerciser to stand on one leg and reach the free leg in multiple directions. This exercise rehabilitates ankle and knee instability, improves dynamic balance, and strengthens the hip stabilizers under real-world perturbation. It is widely used in return-to-sport protocols following lower limb injuries.

execution.starting_position: Stand on one foot with the support knee slightly bent. The free leg is held off the floor. Arms can be used for minimal balance assistance at first.
execution.setup_instructions: No equipment required. Use a smooth floor or balance mat. Mark reach targets on the floor if available.
steps: Step 1: Stand on the support leg with a slight knee bend, maintaining a stable pelvis.
Step 2: Reach the free leg forward (anterior direction) as far as possible while maintaining control of the support leg.
Step 3: Lightly touch the floor with the reaching foot, then return to the starting single-leg stance.
Step 4: Repeat the reach in the posteromedial and posterolateral directions. Complete all reps then switch legs.
execution.breathing_instructions: Breathe naturally and controlled throughout. Avoid breath-holding during the reach.
common_mistakes: Allowing the support knee to collapse inward on each reach
Dropping the hip of the reaching side (Trendelenburg sign)
Placing full weight on the reaching foot instead of a light touch
safety_considerations: Begin with a supported version near a wall if balance is compromised
Consult a physiotherapist for use following ACL reconstruction or ankle sprain rehabilitation
execution.range_of_motion_guidance: Reach as far as control allows in each direction without compromising the stability of the support leg.
execution.tempo_recommendations: 2 seconds for each reach, 2 seconds to return — controlled throughout
coaching_cues: Keep the support knee tracking over the second toe
Do not let the hip of the reaching leg drop
Maintain a tall spine — do not round forward to reach further
